```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```

tidyagsim brings the grammar of [tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org/) to
stochastic simulation studies. If you have tuned a model with `tune_grid()`,
you already know how to run a simulation experiment with it:

| tidymodels | tidyagsim | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| parsnip model spec | simulation spec: `mapping_population()`, `breeding_program()`, `sim_function()` | the simulator and its arguments |
| `tune()` | `tune()` | "let the tuner choose this argument" |
| dials parameters | `extract_parameter_set_dials()`, `n_lines()`, `filial_generation()`, ... | ranges of tuned arguments |
| rsample resamples | `sim_replicates()`, `sim_scenarios()` | paired random seeds and assumption scenarios |
| yardstick `metric_set()` | `sim_metric_set()` | what to measure, and which direction is better |
| `tune_grid()`, `tune_race_anova()`, `tune_bayes()` | `tune_grid()`, `tune_race()`, `tune_bayes()` | how to search |
| `collect_metrics()`, `show_best()`, `select_by_one_std_err()` | same names, plus `pareto_front()`, `compare_designs()` | tidy results |
| workflowsets | `sim_set()`, `sim_map()`, `rank_results()` | comparing several specs at once |

```{r setup}
library(tidyagsim)
```

## A simulation spec

A spec records the arguments of one simulator. The simplest is any R
function that takes its arguments and a `seed` and returns a named list of
outcomes. Here is a toy "trial" whose yield peaks at a seeding rate of 3:

```{r}
trial <- sim_function(
  function(rate, noise, seed) {
    list(yield = 10 - (rate - 3)^2 + rnorm(1, sd = noise), cost = 20 * rate)
  },
  rate = tune(), noise = 1,
  params = list(rate = sim_param(c(0, 6), type = "double", label = "Seeding rate"))
)
trial
```

`tune()` marks `rate` for tuning; `noise` stays fixed. The parameter set is a
dials object, so ranges change with `update()` exactly as in tidymodels:

```{r}
extract_parameter_set_dials(trial)
```

## Replicates are paired seeds

In a simulation, the unit of replication is a random seed. Every design runs
on the *same* seeds (common random numbers), so differences between designs
are paired and much less noisy than independent runs.

```{r}
reps <- sim_replicates(20)
reps
```

## Metrics have directions

```{r}
metrics <- sim_metric_set(sim_metric("yield", "maximize"), cost)
metrics
```

`cost` is built in (minimize); `yield` is defined on the spot.

## Tune

```{r}
res <- tune_grid(trial, reps, grid = 7, metrics = metrics)
res
collect_metrics(res)
```

Every number comes with its Monte Carlo standard error. Pick designs with the
usual helpers:

```{r}
show_best(res, metric = "yield", n = 3)
# The cheapest design within one standard error of the best yield:
select_by_one_std_err(res, cost, metric = "yield")
# Designs no other design beats on both yield and cost:
pareto_front(res)
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Yield and cost against seeding rate, with standard error bars."}
library(ggplot2)
autoplot(res)
```

## Scenarios: robust to what you assumed?

Some inputs are not choices but assumptions. Cross them into scenarios and
every design is run in every scenario:

```{r}
noisy <- sim_replicates(20, scenarios = sim_scenarios(noise = c(0.5, 3)))
res_sc <- tune_grid(trial, noisy, grid = 5, metrics = metrics)
collect_metrics(res_sc) |> subset(.metric == "yield")
```

## Smarter searches

`tune_race()` drops designs that are clearly worse after a few replicates, and
`tune_bayes()` proposes new designs with a Gaussian process. Both answer the
same questions as `tune_grid()` with fewer simulations. With constraints,
`tune_bayes()` searches directly for, say, the cheapest design that keeps
yield above 9:

```{r}
bo <- tune_bayes(trial, sim_replicates(10), metrics = sim_metric_set(cost, sim_metric("yield")),
                 constraints = list(yield = 9), initial = 4, iter = 8)
select_best(bo, metric = "cost", constraints = list(yield = 9))
```

## Real simulators

* `mapping_population()` simulates QTL mapping populations (F2, RIL, BC*s*F*t*,
  NAM, advanced-backcross NAM and MAGIC). See
  `vignette("mapping-design")` for a full study.
* `breeding_program()` runs a breedsim flowchart program with the AlphaSimR
  engine; its fields are tuned by `"stage.field"` path.

## Running big studies

* `control_sim(parallel = TRUE)` runs design batches with the future
  framework (`future::plan(future::multisession)` works on Windows).
* `control_sim(cache = "my-cache")` saves each finished replicate, so a study
  interrupted on a laptop or a cluster resumes where it stopped.
